where: processes in total, including the original
fork() calls executed in sequence by every process
formulas.note: Use as n only the fork() calls that every process reaches; conditional or short-circuit forks need the tree or per-statement factors.

formulas.name: Child processes created by n forks
formulas.note: "How many processes" usually includes the original (2ⁿ); "how many child processes are created" excludes it (2ⁿ − 1).

formulas.name: Lines printed by a fork-then-print loop
where: loop iterations, each doing fork() and then one print
formulas.note: Iteration k runs in 2ᵏ processes. If output is buffered and not flushed before fork(), children inherit the unflushed text and extra copies appear.

formulas.name: Process factors of short-circuit fork expressions
formulas.text: fork() && fork() → ×3; fork() || fork() → ×3; fork() && fork() || fork() → ×5
where: each process that runs the statement ends up as k processes
formulas.note: && evaluates its right side only where the left returned non-zero (the parent); || only where the left returned 0 (the child). Multiply the factors of separate statements.

formulas.name: Capacity of an in/out circular buffer
formulas.text: full ⇔ (in + 1) mod N = out; capacity = N − 1
where: next slot to write and next slot to read; in = out means empty
formulas.note: One slot stays unused so that full and empty look different. Keeping a separate count of items lets all N slots be used.

formulas.name: read() system calls to consume a file to end-of-file
where: read() system calls, including the final one that returns 0
bytes requested per read() (the stdio buffer size, or 1 for byte-at-a-time reads)
formulas.note: The +1 is the call that returns 0 and signals end-of-file; it is needed even when B divides F. Unbuffered 1-byte reads cost F + 1 calls, so buffering cuts the mode switches by roughly a factor of B.

problemTypes.title: Counting processes, children or prints from fork() code
recipe: List the fork() calls that every process reaches; each unconditional fork in straight-line code doubles the count.
For a loop, count the iterations whose condition lets fork() run; that count is the exponent.
For if-conditions and && / ||, follow the parent (non-zero) and the child (0) separately, or multiply per-statement factors (×2, ×3, ×5).
Answer exactly what is asked: total processes, child processes (one fewer) or lines printed.
problemTypes.trap: Children resume where fork() returns, not from the top, and "child processes" excludes the original.

problemTypes.title: Tracing variable values and output after fork()
recipe: Split execution at each fork into a parent branch (return value > 0) and a child branch (return value 0).
Give each branch its own copy of every variable from the moment of the fork; later updates in one branch never reach the other.
Printed addresses are virtual, so parent and child print the same address for a variable even when the values differ.
Output order between parent and child is unspecified unless wait() or other synchronisation forces it.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming the child sees the parent's later updates, or that equal printed addresses mean shared memory.

problemTypes.title: Which process-state transitions are possible
recipe: Draw the five-state diagram with its six edges: admit, dispatch, preempt, block, wake-up and exit.
Check each listed transition against the diagram; Waiting → Running and Ready → Waiting never occur.
Check the scheduling assumption: without preemption, Running → Ready is never forced.
problemTypes.trap: An I/O completion makes the process Ready, not Running; it still waits for the dispatcher.

problemTypes.title: What threads share and what a thread switch saves
recipe: Shared by all threads of a process: code, globals, heap, open files, address space and page tables.
Private to each thread: thread ID, program counter, registers, stack pointer and stack.
A switch between threads of one process saves and restores only the private CPU state; the page-table base stays the same.
problemTypes.trap: Local variables live on the stack, so each thread has its own copy even though the stacks share one address space.

problemTypes.title: True or false statements on user-level and kernel-level threads
recipe: Ask who schedules the threads: a user-space library (ULT) or the kernel (KLT).
Blocking: one ULT blocking in a system call blocks the whole process; one KLT blocking leaves its siblings runnable.
Parallelism: only kernel-visible threads can run on several cores at once. Speed: ULT switches avoid the kernel and are faster.
problemTypes.trap: Swapping the blocking rule: it is user-level threads under many-to-one that all block together.

problemTypes.title: System calls, privileged instructions and mode switches
recipe: Ask whether the operation controls hardware that user code must not touch: I/O devices, the timer, interrupts, the MMU or the mode bit.
If it does, it is privileged and reachable only through a system call; reading the clock or executing the trap instruction is not privileged.
For a library function, ask whether it must enter the kernel (exit, sleep) or can finish in user space (strlen, most malloc calls).
problemTypes.trap: Treating every library call as a system call, or every mode switch as a context switch.

problemTypes.title: Counting system calls or mode switches made by a code fragment
recipe: Mark which calls in the fragment are system calls (read, write, fork, exit) and which are library calls that may batch them (fgetc, printf, malloc).
For buffered I/O, count refills: ⌈F/B⌉ reads of data plus one read that returns 0 at end-of-file.
Each system call is two mode switches (enter and leave the kernel); add a context switch only where the call blocks or the caller is preempted.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting the final read() that returns 0, or counting one system call per fgetc instead of one per buffer refill.

problemTypes.title: Choosing and characterising an IPC mechanism
recipe: Shared memory is fastest after setup and needs explicit synchronisation; message passing goes through the kernel and is simpler to use correctly.
Anonymous pipes need a common ancestor; FIFOs and sockets serve unrelated processes, and sockets also work across machines.
For pipe behaviour, track every open write end: a reader gets end-of-file only when the last one closes.
problemTypes.trap: Believing the kernel synchronises shared memory: once the region is mapped, it no longer mediates any access.

questions.stem: A process executes fork(); fork(); fork(); and every call succeeds. How many processes exist once all three statements have run, counting the original process?
questions.explanation: Every process alive at a fork() executes it, so each call doubles the count: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. That is 2³ = 8 processes, of which 7 are children.

questions.stem: Every fork() in this code succeeds: for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (i % 2 == 0) fork(); How many child processes are created, not counting the original process?
questions.explanation: fork() runs only for i = 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8, and each child inherits i and continues the loop, so every process alive at those iterations forks. Five doublings give 2⁵ = 32 processes, so 32 − 1 = 31 children are created.

questions.stem: A process runs the three statements fork(); then fork() && fork() || fork(); then fork(); and every fork() succeeds. How many processes exist at the end, including the original?
questions.explanation: The first statement turns 1 process into 2. In the second, each process forks; the parent sees non-zero and runs the second fork, whose child sees 0, so its && is false and it runs the third fork; the first child sees 0, skips the second fork and runs the third. Each process becomes 5, giving 2 × 5 = 10. The last fork doubles that to 20.

questions.stem: Two processes share a circular buffer of 8 slots. The producer writes at index in and the consumer reads at index out; the buffer is empty when in == out and full when (in + 1) % 8 == out, and no item counter is kept. What is the largest number of items the buffer can hold at once?
questions.explanation: Filling all 8 slots would make in wrap round to equal out, which is the empty condition. The full test therefore fires one slot early, so the buffer holds at most 8 − 1 = 7 items. A separate count variable would allow all 8.

questions.stem: A program declares int a = 10; and calls fork(), which succeeds. The child executes a = a + 5 and prints the value of a and the address &a as x and y. The parent executes a = a − 5 and prints them as u and v. Which relation holds?
options: u = x + 10 and v = y
u = x + 10 and v ≠ y
u + 10 = x and v = y
u + 10 = x and v ≠ y
questions.explanation: After fork() parent and child own separate copies of a, both starting at 10. The child prints x = 15 and the parent u = 5, so u + 10 = x. Addresses are virtual and the child's address space is a copy of the parent's, so &a is the same virtual address in both (v = y), even though the two copies live in different physical frames.

questions.stem: In the five-state process model with a preemptive scheduler, which of these transitions can occur? I. Running → Ready, II. Ready → Running, III. Blocked → Running, IV. Blocked → Ready.
options: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
II and IV only
questions.explanation: Running → Ready is a preemption, Ready → Running is a dispatch, and Blocked → Ready happens when the awaited event completes. A blocked process never goes straight to Running: it rejoins the ready queue and waits for the dispatcher.

questions.stem: Which statement about user-level threads (many-to-one) and kernel-level threads is false?
options: Switching between user-level threads of one process needs no switch into kernel mode.
Kernel-level threads of one process can run on different cores at the same time.
The kernel is unaware of user-level threads and schedules only their process.
When one kernel-level thread blocks in a system call, every other thread of its process blocks too.
questions.explanation: The kernel schedules each kernel-level thread separately, so when one blocks its siblings stay runnable; that is the main advantage of kernel threads. The other statements are true: user-level switches happen inside the library, kernel threads can run in parallel, and the kernel sees only the process that holds the user-level threads.

questions.stem: In which multithreading model does a blocking system call by one thread stall every thread of the process, with no two threads of the process ever running in parallel?
options: Many-to-one
One-to-one
Many-to-many
Two-level
questions.explanation: Many-to-one maps all user threads onto a single kernel thread, so the kernel can run only one of them at a time, and when that kernel thread blocks, all of them wait. One-to-one, many-to-many and two-level give the other threads further kernel threads to run on.

questions.stem: A parent creates a child and then loops forever without calling wait(). The child exits. Later the parent is killed. What happens to the child?
options: It is an orphan while the parent loops, and is reaped as soon as it exits.
It is a zombie until the parent dies; it is then adopted by init (PID 1), which reaps it.
It is removed from the process table the moment it calls exit.
It stays a zombie permanently, because only its own parent may collect its status.
questions.explanation: An exited child whose status has not been collected is a zombie, so the child stays a zombie while the parent loops. When the parent dies, the child is re-parented to init (PID 1), which waits for adopted children and so removes the zombie's process-table entry.

questions.stem: A process with PID 4200 calls execvp() to run another program, and the call succeeds. Which statement is true?
options: The program runs in a new process with a new PID, and execvp() returns that PID.
The program runs as a child, and the caller resumes after the child exits.
The PID stays 4200, the code, data, heap and stack are replaced, and execvp() never returns.
The PID stays 4200, and execvp() returns 0 once the new program has been loaded.
questions.explanation: exec replaces the program inside the existing process: same PID and parent, open descriptors kept unless marked close-on-exec, but a new code, data, heap and stack. The old code no longer exists, so there is nothing to return to; exec returns −1 only when it fails.

questions.stem: A running process makes a system call that completes without blocking, and no interrupt or preemption occurs meanwhile. What must happen?
options: A switch to kernel mode and back to user mode; no context switch is needed.
A context switch to a kernel process and another one back to the caller.
A context switch, because the PCB must be saved before kernel code can run.
Neither a mode switch nor a context switch, because the call does not block.
questions.explanation: The trap moves the same process into kernel mode, the kernel runs the service on its behalf, and the return-from-trap drops back to user mode. A context switch is needed only when the kernel decides to run a different process, and a non-blocking call with no preemption never forces that.

questions.stem: Two processes on one machine exchange large volumes of data and want the fastest IPC mechanism. Which mechanism fits, and what does it require of them?
options: Shared memory; the processes must synchronise access themselves.
Message passing; the kernel copies each message, so no synchronisation is needed.
Shared memory; the kernel serialises every access to the shared region.
Pipes; the kernel buffer makes them faster than any shared region.
questions.explanation: Once the region is mapped into both address spaces, data moves with ordinary loads and stores and no system call per transfer, which makes shared memory the fastest mechanism. The kernel does not mediate those accesses, so the processes must coordinate with semaphores, mutexes or similar tools.

questions.stem: A parent creates a pipe and forks. The parent closes its read end, writes 100 bytes and closes its write end. The child keeps both of its pipe descriptors open and calls read() in a loop until read() returns 0. What happens to the child?
options: It reads the 100 bytes, then read() returns 0 and the loop ends.
It reads the 100 bytes, then blocks forever in read().
Its first read() returns 0, because the parent has closed its write end.
It is killed by SIGPIPE when it reads from the drained pipe.
questions.explanation: read() on an empty pipe returns 0 only when no write end is open anywhere. The child still holds its own inherited write descriptor, so after draining the 100 bytes it blocks waiting for data that can never arrive; it should close its unused write end first. SIGPIPE is sent to writers when no read end is open, never to readers.

questions.stem: The CPU switches from one thread to another thread of the same process. Which of the following must be saved for the outgoing thread and reloaded for the incoming one?
options: The page-table base register
The stack pointer
The program counter
The general-purpose registers
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack, program counter and register values, so these make up the per-thread context a switch saves and restores. Both threads run in the same address space, so the page-table base register keeps its value; skipping that change is why a thread switch is cheaper than a process switch.

questions.stem: Which of these C library calls always enter the kernel through a system call?
options: exit(0)
malloc(16)
sleep(1)
strlen(s)
questions.explanation: exit(0) must ask the kernel to end the process, and sleep(1) must ask the kernel to suspend the process and wake it a second later, so both always trap. strlen(s) only scans memory in user space. malloc(16) usually hands out memory the allocator already holds, and enters the kernel (brk or mmap) only when the heap must grow.

questions.stem: A program reads a 10,000-byte file to end-of-file in two versions. Version A calls fgetc() until it returns EOF; the stdio library refills its 4096-byte buffer with one read() system call each time the buffer is empty. Version B calls read(fd, &c, 1) until it returns 0. Counting in each version the final read() that returns 0, how many more read() system calls does version B make than version A?
questions.explanation: Version A: the refills return 4096, 4096 and 1808 bytes, and a fourth read() returns 0, so ⌈10000/4096⌉ + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4 calls. Version B: one call per byte plus the call that returns 0, 10000 + 1 = 10001 calls. The difference is 10001 − 4 = 9997. Each of those calls costs two mode switches, which is why buffered library I/O is so much faster.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be privileged instructions, executable only in kernel mode?
options: Read the time-of-day clock
Set the interval timer
Execute the trap (system call) instruction
Disable interrupts
questions.explanation: Setting the timer or disabling interrupts would let a user program keep the CPU and stop the OS from regaining control, so both are privileged. Reading the clock harms nobody, and the trap instruction must work in user mode because it is how a user program enters the kernel.

pitfalls.text: fork() returns twice, 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent, and the child resumes where the fork() call returns, not at the top of main.
A zombie has exited but not been reaped; an orphan is still running after its parent died. They are different states with different fixes: wait() in the parent, or adoption by init.
Under many-to-one, one user-level thread blocking in a system call blocks the whole process; a kernel-level thread blocks only itself.
Threads share code, globals, heap and open files, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter, so local variables are per-thread.
n forks give 2ⁿ processes but only 2ⁿ − 1 children: check whether the question counts the original process.
A mode switch into the kernel is not a context switch: a system call that does not block normally returns to the same process, unless the kernel preempts it on the way out.
Parent and child print the same address for a variable yet hold different values: the address is virtual and the memory is not shared.
A blocked process goes to Ready when its event completes, never straight to Running.

errata.claim: The process states form the chain New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated.
errata.correction: The states form a cycle, not a chain. A Waiting process returns to Ready when its event completes, never straight to Running; a Running process can also be preempted back to Ready; and Terminated is normally entered from Running when the process exits.

errata.claim: Signals are asynchronous notifications, with SIGINT, SIGKILL and SIGSEGV as examples.
errata.correction: SIGSEGV is a synchronous signal: like SIGFPE, it is raised by the process's own faulting instruction and delivered to that process. SIGINT, SIGKILL, SIGTERM and SIGALRM are asynchronous, sent from outside the process at an unpredictable point.

errata.claim: Signals are asynchronous notifications used for events such as keyboard interrupts or fatal errors.
errata.correction: The keyboard interrupt (SIGINT) is asynchronous, but fatal-error signals such as SIGSEGV and SIGFPE are synchronous: they are caused by an instruction of the receiving process itself.
